claims.text: A conventionally fabricated W–Cu composite has a random, isotropic distribution of tungsten and copper phases.
Directional solidification can produce an oriented, continuous copper phase in a W–Cu composite.
Directional solidification promotes alignment of the copper phase.
Copper-phase alignment increases the continuity of high-thermal-conductivity pathways through the composite.
Aligned, continuous copper channels reduce W–Cu thermal boundary resistance and interface scattering.
Reduced interface scattering and thermal resistance increase the effective thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites.
The tungsten phase provides inherent mechanical strength.
The tungsten phase provides inherent irradiation resilience.
Retaining the tungsten phase's properties will allow copper alignment to preserve the composite's mechanical durability.
Retaining the tungsten phase's properties will allow copper alignment to preserve the composite's irradiation resistance.

A directionally solidified W–Cu composite with aligned copper will have roughly 10–20% higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable composite with isotropically dispersed copper.
The directionally solidified composite will retain mechanical durability similar to that of a conventionally processed W–Cu composite.
The directionally solidified composite will retain irradiation resistance similar to that of a conventionally processed W–Cu composite.
The predicted benefits should hold at moderate to high temperatures under irradiation representative of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
The thermal-conductivity benefit requires tightly controlled processing that creates a continuous copper network.
Incomplete copper alignment may prevent the predicted thermal-conductivity improvement.
Extreme irradiation or temperature gradients may disrupt the aligned copper network and eliminate its benefits.
